cell-communication-s1.title: Light from bacteria at increasing cell density
cell-communication-s1.html:
The marine bacterium Vibrio fischeri makes light with an enzyme called luciferase. Researchers grew three strains in flasks of seawater medium at 25 °C and measured cell density and light output as each culture grew. Strain W is the wild type. Strain N lacks the enzyme that makes the bacterium's autoinducer. Strain N+A is strain N grown with 5 µM synthetic autoinducer added to the medium at the start. Light per cell is given relative to strain W at the lowest density (set to 1). Points are means of 3 flasks.

cell-communication-s2.title: How far does an injected dye spread?
cell-communication-s2.html:
Researchers grew a single flat layer of liver cells in a dish. They injected one cell with a fluorescent dye and, 5 minutes later, counted how many neighboring cells had become fluorescent. They tested four dyes of different sizes, in untreated cells and in cells given a drug that closes gap junctions 10 minutes before the injection. Each value is the mean for 10 injected cells.

cell-communication-s3.title: Does a T cell need to touch?
cell-communication-s3.html:
Helper T cells are white blood cells that become active when their receptor binds an antigen, a fragment of a pathogen's protein, displayed on the surface of an antigen-presenting cell. Researchers set up culture wells containing helper T cells that recognize one antigen. In some wells antigen-presenting cells were mixed in with the T cells. In others the two cell types were separated by a filter with pores 0.4 µm wide, which lets dissolved molecules through but not cells. After 24 hours they measured the percentage of T cells that had become active.

signal-transduction-intro-s1.title: Two hormones, two receptors
signal-transduction-intro-s1.html:
Researchers studied two hormones that act on the same kind of cultured cell. Hormone X is a small protein; hormone Y is a steroid. To find where each binds, they added radioactively labeled hormone, broke the cells open and measured how much label was bound to plasma membranes and how much to the nucleus. In other dishes they attached each hormone to plastic beads far too large to enter cells, or added a drug that stops cells from making new mRNA. Responses are given as a percentage of the response to the free hormone with no drug (means of 4 dishes).

signal-transduction-pathways-s3.title: Three versions of a growth factor receptor
signal-transduction-pathways-s3.html:
A growth factor acts through a receptor tyrosine kinase. Researchers put one of three versions of the receptor gene into cultured cells that lack the receptor: the normal version; version D, which has a mutation that lets two receptors pair up without the growth factor; and version K, which has a mutation that destroys the receptor's kinase activity. They measured the percentage of receptors phosphorylated on tyrosine, the activity of a relay kinase further down the pathway, and the percentage of cells that divided in 24 hours, with and without growth factor (means of 3 cultures).

At several times after exposure they measured the percentage of cells in G1 and the percentage dying by apoptosis. A third set of dishes of each line was not exposed. Values are means of 3 dishes.

cell-cycle-regulation-s3.title: Fusing cells in different phases
cell-cycle-regulation-s3.html:
In the 1970s, researchers fused pairs of mammalian cells that were in different phases of the cell cycle. Each fused cell had two nuclei sharing one cytoplasm. They then watched what the second nucleus did.

Results of fusing a cell in one phase with a cell in another
Cells fusedWhat the second nucleus did
S-phase cell + G1 cellThe G1 nucleus began copying its DNA at once, hours earlier than it would have alone.
S-phase cell + G2 cellThe G2 nucleus did not copy its DNA again; it waited until the S nucleus finished, then both entered mitosis.
M-phase cell + G1 cellThe G1 nucleus's envelope broke down and its uncopied chromosomes condensed at once, as single chromatids.
M-phase cell + G2 cellThe G2 nucleus's envelope broke down and its chromosomes condensed at once, each as two sister chromatids.

items.q: Which statement best describes how light per cell in strain W changes as cell density increases?
options: It stays near 1 up to 3 × 10⁸ cells/mL, rises steeply from about 4 to 7 × 10⁸, then levels off.
It rises in proportion to density, so each doubling of density roughly doubles the light made by each cell.
It rises steeply at the lowest densities and then falls as the culture becomes more crowded.
It stays close to 1 at each density, because the light made by a cell depends on its own luciferase.

items.q: By what factor does light per cell in strain W increase between 3 × 10⁸ and 6 × 10⁸ cells/mL? Give a whole number.
Which comparison gives the strongest evidence that strain N can still detect the autoinducer and make light?
options: Strain N+A with strain N at the same low density
Strain N with strain W at 10 × 10⁸ cells/mL
Strain W at 1 × 10⁸ with strain W at 8 × 10⁸ cells/mL
Strain N at 1 × 10⁸ with strain N at 8 × 10⁸ cells/mL

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for strain W's dim light at low density and bright light at high density?
options: Each cell releases autoinducer slowly; only when many cells share the volume does its concentration bind enough receptors to switch the light genes on.
Crowded cells run short of nutrients, and starving cells make light as a stress response that well-fed cells at low density do not show.
Light from neighboring cells is absorbed and released again by each cell, so each cell appears brighter when many cells surround it.
Cells that have divided many times have built up luciferase over each division, so older, denser cultures glow more per cell.

items.q: A fourth strain, R, makes autoinducer normally but lacks the receptor protein for it. Predict the light per cell of strain R grown with 5 µM added autoinducer.
options: Close to 1 at each density, because the autoinducer has nothing to bind in strain R
About 600 at each density, like strain N+A, because the autoinducer is present from the start
Close to 1 at low density, rising to about 650 at high density, like strain W
Higher than strain W at each density, because strain R gets autoinducer from two sources

items.q: Which statement best describes the results in untreated cells?
options: Dyes P and Q (457 daltons or less) reached over 20 neighbors; dyes R and S reached none.
Each dye reached about the same number of neighbors, whatever its size.
The larger the dye, the more neighboring cells it reached in 5 minutes.
Dye P reached fewer neighbors than dye S, because small dyes leak out of cells before they can spread.

items.q: Calculate the percent decrease in the number of neighbors reached by dye P when the gap-junction blocker is added. Give a whole number.
Which claim is best supported by the data?
options: Molecules below a size limit between about 460 and 3,000 daltons pass from cell to cell through gap junctions within minutes.
Gap junctions pump small dyes into neighboring cells using ATP, and the blocker works by stopping ATP production.
The dyes leak out of the injected cell and are taken up from the medium by its neighbors.
Large dyes do reach the neighbors through gap junctions, but more slowly than small dyes do.

items.q: What is the main reason for including the cells given the gap-junction blocker?
options: To test whether the dye spreads through gap junctions rather than by some other route
To make sure the injected cell was still alive and healthy after the injection was made
To keep the size of the dye the same from one trial to the next
To measure how quickly each dye diffuses through the cytoplasm

items.q: Heart muscle cells are joined by gap junctions that let ions flow between them. Predict the effect of the same blocker on a sheet of beating heart muscle cells.
options: Their contractions would fall out of step, because the electrical change could not pass from cell to cell.
Each cell would contract faster, because ions could no longer escape into neighboring cells.
The cells would stop making ATP, because glucose could no longer enter them.
There would be no change in the beat, because hormones carried in the blood set the timing of each contraction.

items.q: Which conclusion is best supported by wells 3 and 4?
options: Activation needs contact with the presenting cells; molecules they release into the medium are not enough.
The filter killed most of the T cells, so they could not become active.
Antigen-presenting cells release a dissolved signal into the medium that activates T cells across the filter.
The antigen alone activates T cells, and the antigen-presenting cells play no part.

items.q: What possibility does well 2 rule out?
options: That touching an antigen-presenting cell activates T cells even when no antigen is displayed
That T cells become active on their own during 24 hours in culture
That the antigen is toxic to T cells at the concentration used
That the filter holds back dissolved molecules from the medium as well as the cells themselves

items.q: In a fifth well, cells are mixed and antigen is added, but the antigen-presenting cells were first given a drug that stops them displaying antigen fragments on their surface. They still take in the antigen. Predict the percentage of active T cells.
options: Low, close to well 2, because the T cells touch presenting cells but find no antigen displayed
High, close to well 3, because the antigen is still inside the presenting cells
High, close to well 3, because the presenting cells can still release signals into the medium
Intermediate, between wells 3 and 4, because half of the signal is still delivered

items.q: The body has helper T cells with millions of different receptors, each fitting a different antigen. How does requiring contact with a presenting cell make the immune response specific to the pathogen that is actually present?
options: Only T cells whose receptor fits the displayed antigen bind and become active, so the response is built from cells that recognize this pathogen.
Contact lets the presenting cell hand its own receptors to each T cell it touches, giving them the right shape.
Contact lets the antigen-presenting cell destroy T cells whose receptors do not fit the antigen.
A released signal would travel too slowly through the blood to reach T cells in time, so contact is faster.

items.q: Which is an example of endocrine signaling?
options: The pancreas releases insulin into the blood, and it acts on muscle cells in the legs.
A neuron releases a neurotransmitter that binds receptors on the muscle cell next to it.
Two neighboring plant cells exchange sugar through plasmodesmata in their cell walls.
Platelets at a cut release a growth factor that makes nearby skin cells divide.

items.q: In a strain of mice, the muscle cells lack one protein. After a meal these mice release insulin normally and it reaches their muscle cells, yet the muscle cells do not respond to it. Which missing protein best explains this?
options: The receptor protein on the muscle cell surface that insulin binds
An enzyme in the blood that breaks insulin down after a meal
A channel that lets insulin pass into the muscle cell's nucleus
The protein in the pancreas that releases insulin by exocytosis

items.q: At a wound, platelets release a growth factor that is normally broken down by enzymes in the tissue fluid within minutes. Predict the effect of a drug that slows this breakdown.
options: Cells farther from the wound would bind the growth factor and start to divide.
Cells near the wound would stop dividing, because the growth factor would stay outside them.
The growth factor would enter the blood and act as a hormone on target cells in organs throughout the body.
No change, because the platelets themselves are the cells with receptors for the growth factor.

items.q: Select the two features that make synaptic signaling faster and more precisely aimed than endocrine signaling.
options: The neurotransmitter crosses a gap of a few tens of nanometers instead of traveling through the blood.
The neurotransmitter is released right next to a single target cell.
Neurotransmitters are much larger molecules than hormones.
Neurotransmitters act without binding to receptors.
The neurotransmitter enters the blood, which carries it quickly to its target.

items.q: A small fluorescent sugar injected into one leaf cell appears in the neighboring cells within minutes, even though every plant cell is surrounded by a cell wall. Which structure best explains this?
options: Plasmodesmata, channels through the cell walls that join the cytoplasms of neighboring cells
Aquaporins, membrane channels that let water and dissolved sugars cross into the cell wall
Vesicles that release the sugar into the cell wall by exocytosis, followed by uptake into the next cell
A hormone that carries the sugar through the plant to cells with receptors

items.q: Put the events of synaptic signaling from a neuron to a muscle cell in order.
options: An electrical signal reaches the end of the neuron.
Vesicles fuse with the neuron's membrane and release neurotransmitter by exocytosis.
The neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft.
The neurotransmitter binds receptor proteins on the muscle cell.
The muscle cell's behavior changes and it contracts.

items.q: Which statement is best supported by the binding data?
options: X binds mainly at the plasma membrane and Y mainly in the nucleus.
X and Y both bind mainly at the plasma membrane, but Y also enters the nucleus.
X binds mainly in the nucleus and Y mainly at the plasma membrane of the cell.
Neither hormone binds the cells strongly, since less than 100% of the label is found.

items.q: Which result most directly shows that hormone Y must get inside the cell to act?
options: Y attached to beads too large to enter cells gives 3% of the normal response.
Y's first response takes 45 minutes, compared with 30 seconds for hormone X.
With the drug that blocks mRNA synthesis, Y gives just 4% of the normal response.
Hormone Y is a steroid, while hormone X is a small protein.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the difference in response time between the two hormones?
options: Y switches genes on, so new mRNA and proteins must be made; X changes the activity of existing proteins.
Y is a larger molecule than X, so it diffuses through the tissue fluid more slowly before reaching the cells.
Y is broken down inside the cell before it acts, while X acts as soon as it enters the cytoplasm.
Fewer cells have receptors for Y, so it takes longer for enough cells to respond to measure a change.

items.q: Cells are given a drug that blocks the protein kinases they contain. Predict how the drug affects the responses to X and Y.
options: X's response is greatly reduced; Y's is affected much less.
Y's response is greatly reduced; X's is affected much less.
Both responses are unchanged, because kinases act after reception.
Both responses rise, because the receptors stay bound for longer.

items.q: A third hormone, Z, is a small nonpolar molecule. Which prediction for Z is best supported by reasoning from these results?
options: Like Y, it binds mainly in the nucleus and is blocked by the mRNA drug.
Like X, it binds mainly to plasma membranes and is unaffected by beads.
It binds both places equally and responds in 30 seconds whether on beads or not.
It does not bind any receptor, since nonpolar molecules pass straight through cells.

items.q: By what factor does the number of active molecules increase from the relay protein step to the kinase 2 step? Give a whole number.
At which step does the number of active molecules fall instead of rise, and why?
options: At kinase 1, because several second messenger molecules must bind to switch on each kinase.
At the relay protein, because one receptor can switch on just one relay protein at a time.
At kinase 2, because each kinase 1 molecule is used up when it phosphorylates a protein.
At the product, because the target enzyme is a ligand that leaves the cell after it is made.

items.q: A drug halves the number of relay proteins each bound receptor switches on, from 20 to 10. Predict the product made per minute per receptor.
options: 250,000,000, half the original, because each later step multiplies whatever it receives
499,999,990, almost unchanged, because just 10 relay proteins out of the whole chain are lost
500,000,000, unchanged, because the later steps make up for the loss
5,000,000, a hundredth of the original, because the loss is amplified at each step

items.q: The ligand for this pathway is present in the blood at about 10⁻¹⁰ mol/L, so each liver cell has only a few receptors bound at a time. How does the model explain why such a low concentration still produces a large response?
options: Each bound receptor leads to about 5 × 10⁸ product molecules a minute, because every step multiplies the signal.
The few bound ligand molecules are copied inside the cell until there are enough to switch on each relay protein.
The liver cell stores the ligand until its concentration inside the cell reaches the level needed for a response.
At low ligand concentration each receptor binds many ligand molecules at once, which multiplies its effect.

items.q: In cells given a drug that blocks the phosphatase acting on kinase 2, the ligand is washed away after one minute. Predict product formation over the next 30 minutes.
options: It continues much longer than normal, because kinase 2 stays phosphorylated.
It stops at once, because the phosphatase is needed to switch kinase 2 on.
It stops at once, because product can be made just while the ligand remains bound.
It rises steadily for the whole 30 minutes, because second messengers keep forming.

items.q: Which statement best describes protein K in the no-drug dishes after the ligand is washed away?
options: Phosphorylated K falls from 80% to under 10% within about 10 minutes of washing.
Phosphorylated K stays near 80% for the rest of the experiment.
Phosphorylated K falls slowly and steadily, reaching 3% at 40 minutes.
Phosphorylated K rises further, peaking at 17 minutes.

items.q: Calculate the average rate at which the percentage of phosphorylated K falls between 15 and 20 minutes in the no-drug dishes. Give a whole number of percentage points per minute.
Which explanation is best supported by comparing the no-drug and phosphatase-blocker dishes after 15 minutes?
options: Phosphatases remove the phosphate from K, so K switches off once the kinase stops adding new phosphate.
K loses its phosphate on its own, so the phosphatase blocker damages K in a way that locks the phosphate on.
Washing removes K from the cells, so less of it is left to carry phosphate.
The ligand is still bound after washing, so K stays phosphorylated in both sets of dishes.

items.q: Which result supports the claim that K is phosphorylated by a kinase in the pathway, and not by some other process?
options: With the kinase blocker, K stays below 5% phosphorylated even though the ligand is present.
With no drug, K reaches 80% phosphorylated within 10 minutes of adding ligand.
With the phosphatase blocker, K stays above 80% after the ligand is washed away.
In each set of dishes, about 2-3% of K is phosphorylated before ligand is added.

items.q: What mainly decides whether a signaling molecule's receptor is on the cell surface or inside the cell?
options: Whether the molecule can cross the lipid bilayer, given its size and polarity
Whether the molecule arrives in the blood or diffuses over from a nearby cell
How high the molecule's concentration is in the fluid outside the cell
Whether the response that the cell gives to the signal is a fast or a slow one

items.q: In liver cells, one hormone causes glycogen breakdown within 20 seconds and, over the next 3 hours, an increase in the amount of an enzyme that makes glucose. The fast response is unaffected by a drug that blocks mRNA synthesis, but the slow response is prevented. Which explanation best fits?
options: The pathway branches: one branch switches on enzymes already present, another switches genes on.
The hormone binds a surface receptor for the fast response, then enters the nucleus for the slow one.
The fast response uses up the hormone, so the slow response begins after a second dose arrives.
The drug slows the cell's metabolism, which delays the slow response but does not reach the fast one.

items.q: A cell line makes a version of a surface receptor whose binding site has a slightly different shape, so the usual ligand binds it far more weakly. The ligand is added at its normal concentration. Predict each change, compared with normal cells.

variables.name: Fraction of receptors with ligand bound
Activity of the first relay protein
Number of receptor proteins in the membrane
Response to a second hormone that uses its own, unchanged receptor and pathway

items.q: Select the two statements that correctly describe second messengers.
options: They are small non-protein molecules or ions that diffuse quickly through the cytoplasm.
They are made or released in large numbers inside the cell when a receptor is activated.
They are the ligands that bind cell-surface receptors from outside the cell.
They travel in the blood to carry the signal from one organ to another.
They are enzymes that add phosphate groups to relay proteins.

items.q: Cells are engineered to make a version of a steroid's intracellular receptor that binds the steroid normally but cannot enter the nucleus. Predict the effect of adding the steroid.
options: The steroid enters and binds the receptor, but the genes it normally switches on stay off.
The steroid is unable to get into the cells, because its receptor is stuck in the cytoplasm.
The genes are switched on as usual, because the steroid itself diffuses into the nucleus.
The steroid binds a cell-surface receptor instead and switches the genes on through kinases.

items.q: Put the steps of a steroid hormone's action in order.
options: The hormone diffuses across the plasma membrane.
The hormone binds a receptor protein in the cytoplasm.
The hormone-receptor complex moves into the nucleus.
The complex binds DNA and switches particular genes on.
New mRNA is made and new proteins are built from it.
The cell's behavior changes.

items.q: Compared with hormone alone, how does the phosphodiesterase inhibitor change the cAMP curve?
options: cAMP rises more steeply and levels off at almost three times the hormone-only level.
cAMP rises to the same level, but reaches it about twice as fast.
cAMP stays near the starting level for the whole 20 minutes.
cAMP rises to the same peak as with hormone alone, then falls back to the start.

items.q: At 8 minutes, by what percentage is cAMP higher with the phosphodiesterase inhibitor than with hormone only? Give a whole number.
Which explanation best accounts for the fall in cAMP after the antagonist is added at 10 minutes?
options: Fewer receptors are active, so adenylyl cyclase slows, while phosphodiesterase keeps breaking cAMP down.
The antagonist binds cAMP inside the cells and carries it out across the membrane into the medium.
The antagonist switches phosphodiesterase on, which speeds up the breakdown of cAMP already in the cell.
Hormone H is used up by its receptors after 10 minutes, so the antagonist just speeds a fall already starting.

items.q: With hormone only, cAMP stays at 50 pmol/mg from 6 to 20 minutes. Which result is the best evidence that cAMP is being made and broken down continuously during that time?
options: After the antagonist is added, cAMP falls from 50 to 12 within 5 minutes.
With the adenylyl cyclase inhibitor, cAMP stays at about 5 throughout.
With the hormone alone, cAMP rises from 5 to 48 in the first 2 minutes of the experiment.
Each of the four curves starts from about the same cAMP level at time 0.

items.q: Predict glucose release by the cells given hormone H plus the adenylyl cyclase inhibitor, compared with hormone only.
options: Much lower, near untreated cells, because with no cAMP made, protein kinase A stays switched off.
About the same, because the hormone still binds its receptor and switches on G proteins.
Higher, because ATP that would have become cAMP is used to release more glucose.
About the same, because glucose release depends on glycogen stores, not on cAMP.

items.q: Which comparison best shows that cAMP acts after the receptor in the pathway?
options: Treatments 6 and 7: the antagonist blocks epinephrine's effect but not that of membrane-crossing cAMP.
Treatments 2 and 3: epinephrine and membrane-crossing cAMP release about the same amount of glucose.
Treatments 4 and 5: the protein kinase A inhibitor blocks the effects of both epinephrine and membrane-crossing cAMP.
Treatments 1 and 2: epinephrine raises glucose release from 4 to 38 µmol per gram of liver.

items.q: What does treatment 5 show that treatment 4 alone does not?
options: Protein kinase A is needed after cAMP, not just somewhere after the receptor.
The protein kinase A inhibitor does not damage the liver slices in any lasting way.
Membrane-crossing cAMP gets into liver cells as fast as epinephrine binds its receptor.
The receptor antagonist and the kinase inhibitor act on the same protein in the pathway.

items.q: How many times as much glucose do slices release with epinephrine as with no treatment? Give your answer to one decimal place.
Liver slices from an animal with a mutation in the G protein that stops it binding GTP are tested. Predict glucose release with epinephrine alone and with membrane-crossing cAMP alone.
options: About 4 with epinephrine and about 36 with cAMP
About 38 with epinephrine and about 36 with cAMP
About 4 with epinephrine and about 4 with cAMP
About 38 with epinephrine and about 4 with cAMP

items.q: Using the data and what you know about this pathway, put the components in the order the signal passes through them.
options: Epinephrine receptor
G protein
Adenylyl cyclase making cAMP
Protein kinase A
Glycogen breakdown and glucose release

items.q: Which statement best describes cells with receptor version D?
options: They are about as active without growth factor as with it, at each level measured.
Their receptors are active without growth factor, but their relay kinase is not.
They divide just when growth factor is present, in the same way as cells with the normal receptor.
They are less active than normal cells, with or without growth factor.

items.q: Version K binds the growth factor normally. Which explanation best accounts for its results?
options: Without kinase activity the receptors cannot phosphorylate each other, so relay proteins are not switched on.
Version K is unable to pair up when the growth factor binds, so its kinase parts do not come close enough to act.
Version K's kinase works but does not reach the cell surface, so it does not meet the growth factor in the medium.
Version K is phosphorylated normally, but the relay kinase is missing from these particular cells.

items.q: Cells with version D are given a drug that blocks the kinase activity of this receptor. Predict the percentage of cells that divide in 24 hours without growth factor.
options: About 4%, because the paired receptors still need kinase activity to signal
About 35%, because version D pairs up without growth factor whatever the drug does
About 70%, because blocking the kinase traps the receptors in their paired state
About 38%, because the drug acts on normal receptors but not on the version D receptors

items.q: Which receptor version, if it arose in a person's skin cells, would be most likely to contribute to cancer, and why?
options: Version D, because it drives division even without growth factor.
Version K, because cells that do not respond to growth factor are no longer under control.
Version D, because it binds growth factor more strongly than the normal receptor does.
Neither, because a change in a receptor does not affect steps further down the pathway.

items.q: Cells use ATP to pump Ca²⁺ out of the cytoplasm, keeping its concentration there about 10,000 times lower than in the ER. How does this make Ca²⁺ an effective second messenger?
options: Opening a few channels lets Ca²⁺ diffuse in down its steep gradient, raising its level many-fold in milliseconds.
The pumps add a phosphate group to each Ca²⁺ ion as they move it, which switches the ion on so it can bind proteins.
Keeping Ca²⁺ inside the ER lets the ER release Ca²⁺ into the blood when a hormone signal is needed.
Low Ca²⁺ in the cytoplasm keeps most enzymes in the cell switched on until a signal raises the level.

items.q: Propranolol binds one of epinephrine's receptors on heart muscle cells without activating it. Predict how a person taking propranolol responds to a sudden scare.
options: The rise in heart rate is smaller, because fewer receptors are free to bind epinephrine.
The rise in heart rate is larger, because propranolol adds to the effect of epinephrine.
The heart rate rises as usual, because propranolol binds outside the receptor's binding site.
The heart rate rises as usual, because epinephrine enters heart cells without needing a receptor.

items.q: A mutation changes a liver cell's G protein so it binds GTP normally but hydrolyzes it to GDP extremely slowly. Predict cAMP in the cells 20 minutes after epinephrine has been washed away.
options: It stays high, because switched-on G proteins stay on and keep adenylyl cyclase active.
It returns to normal, because the receptor is no longer bound by epinephrine.
It returns to normal, because phosphodiesterase works faster in cells with this mutation.
It falls below normal, because GTP is used up by the mutant G proteins.

items.q: Select the two changes that would keep glycogen breakdown going in a liver cell for longer than normal after epinephrine is removed.
options: Phosphodiesterase is blocked by a drug.
The G protein cannot hydrolyze GTP.
A receptor antagonist is added.
Adenylyl cyclase is missing.
Protein kinase A is blocked by a drug.

items.q: Cholera toxin enters the cells lining the intestine and changes their G protein so that it cannot hydrolyze GTP. Predict each change in an infected person's gut cells, compared with uninfected cells.

variables.name: Fraction of G proteins in the active, GTP-bound form
Water moving out of the cells into the gut
Amount of adenylyl cyclase protein in the cells

items.q: Put the events that follow epinephrine binding to a liver cell in order.
options: The receptor changes shape.
The G protein releases GDP and binds GTP.
The G protein switches on adenylyl cyclase.
Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP into cAMP.
cAMP switches on protein kinase A.
Protein kinase A phosphorylates the next kinase in the cascade.

items.q: Which statement best describes the hormones after each meal?
options: Insulin rises and falls with glucose, while glucagon falls and then recovers.
Insulin and glucagon both rise with glucose and both fall as glucose falls back.
Glucagon rises with glucose, while insulin stays near its fasting level through the day.
Insulin rises an hour before glucose rises, in step with the time of each meal.

items.q: Calculate the percent increase in blood glucose from 12:00 to 13:00. Give a whole number.
Which explanation best accounts for the changes between 15:00 and 17:00?
options: Running muscles took up glucose; the fall triggered glucagon release and less insulin, so the liver released glucose.
Running used up the insulin in the blood, so glucose fell; glucagon then rose to take the place of the missing insulin.
The run raised insulin, which lowered glucose; glucagon rose afterward because glucose had become too high.
Glucagon rose first and caused glucose to fall, and glucose recovered at 17:00 because the next meal began.

items.q: Predict the glucose curve after lunch for a person with untreated type 1 diabetes, compared with this volunteer.
options: It rises higher and stays high for hours, because little insulin is released to trigger glucose uptake.
It rises to the same peak but falls back faster, because the person's cells absorb glucose without insulin.
It stays flat, because without insulin the person's gut is unable to absorb glucose from the meal.
It rises to the same peak and falls at the same rate, because glucagon takes over insulin's job.

items.q: Which feature of the data is the best evidence that blood glucose is controlled by negative feedback?
options: After each rise or fall, glucose returns to about 85-90 mg/dL as the opposing hormone acts.
Glucose reaches about the same peak, 138-142 mg/dL, after each of the three meals of the day.
Insulin is higher at 19:00 than at any earlier time of day.
Glucagon is about 90 pg/mL at 6:00 and about 89 pg/mL at 22:00.

items.q: Which statement best describes person C compared with person A?
options: C has higher insulin and higher glucose at every time point.
C has lower insulin but higher glucose at each of the time points.
C has higher insulin, so C's glucose returns to fasting faster.
C has the same insulin as A, but higher glucose throughout.

items.q: Which person most likely has type 1 diabetes, and what is the best evidence?
options: Person B, whose insulin stays at 2-3 µU/mL as glucose climbs to 320 mg/dL
Person C, whose glucose is still above 200 mg/dL two hours after the drink
Person B, whose fasting glucose is the highest of the three at 160 mg/dL
Person A, whose insulin falls back to 20 µU/mL by the end of the test

items.q: At 60 minutes, how many times as much insulin does person C have as person A? Give your answer to one decimal place.
Why does person C's insulin keep rising between 60 and 120 minutes?
options: C's target cells respond weakly to insulin, so glucose stays high and keeps stimulating the beta cells.
C's beta cells release insulin at a fixed rate that does not depend on the level of glucose.
C's liver turns the glucose from the drink into insulin, so more glucose means more insulin.
C's insulin keeps rising because glucagon release has stopped and insulin replaces it.

items.q: Persons B and C are each given the same dose of insulin by injection after the test. Predict the effect on their glucose.
options: B's glucose falls a lot, and C's falls less, because C's cells respond weakly to insulin.
C's glucose falls a lot, and B's falls less, because B's cells have lost their insulin receptors.
Neither glucose level falls, because diabetes damages the liver rather than the hormone system.
Both fall by the same amount, because injected insulin works the same way in each person.

items.q: Which statement best describes ethylene from group 1?
options: It stays low for about 3 days, rises steeply to a peak on day 6, then declines.
It rises at a steady rate from day 0 to day 8.
It peaks on day 3 and then falls steadily to day 8.
It stays below 1 µL per kg per hour throughout.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the shape of the group 1 curve between days 3 and 6?
options: Ethylene binding the fruit's receptors makes the fruit produce more ethylene, so production speeds itself up.
The bananas lose water as they age, so the ethylene in them becomes more concentrated each day.
Ethylene production is set by the day of harvest, so each banana starts producing heavily on day 4.
Ethylene breaks down cell walls, and the broken walls release ethylene that had been stored in them.

items.q: Which result best supports the claim that the rise in ethylene depends on the bananas detecting ethylene?
options: Group 3, whose ethylene receptors were blocked by 1-MCP, stays below 0.5.
Group 2, kept with ripe bananas, reaches its peak 3 days earlier than group 1.
Group 2 reaches a slightly higher peak than group 1, by about 1 µL per kg per hour.
Each of the three groups starts at the same ethylene level, 0.2, on day 0.

items.q: A grocer finds one overripe banana in a box of green ones. Using the data, predict what happens to the rest of the box if it stays.
options: They ripen days sooner, because ethylene from the ripe banana starts their own ethylene burst.
The green bananas ripen on the same schedule, because each fruit ripens on its own internal timer.
The green bananas ripen more slowly, because the ripe banana uses up the ethylene in the box.
Just the bananas touching the ripe one ripen sooner, because ethylene passes by direct contact.

items.q: On a hot day, nerve endings in the skin detect rising temperature, a region of the brain compares it with 37 °C, and sweat glands release sweat. In this loop, the sweat glands are the
options: effectors
sensors
control center
stimulus

items.q: During an infection, chemicals from immune cells raise the brain's temperature set point from 37 °C to 39 °C. Predict what a person feels and does while their temperature is still 37 °C.
options: They feel cold and shiver, because the control center now reads 37 °C as below the set point.
They feel hot and sweat, because the infection itself is producing heat inside the body.
They feel nothing, because their temperature has not changed from its normal value.
They feel hot and sweat, because a higher set point makes the sensors more sensitive to heat.

items.q: When a blood vessel is cut, platelets stick at the cut and release chemicals that make more platelets stick. Which statement best explains why this positive feedback loop does not keep growing through the bloodstream?
options: Once the clot seals the break, the exposed damaged wall that started the loop is covered, so the stimulus ends.
Platelets in the blood are used up after the first few seconds of clotting.
A negative feedback loop takes over as soon as clotting starts and reverses it.
Positive feedback loops weaken with each cycle until they stop by themselves.

items.q: Select the two examples of negative feedback.
options: Insulin release rises after a meal, and glucose falls back to its normal range.
Sweating increases as body temperature rises above 37 °C, cooling the body.
Oxytocin release rises as contractions stretch the cervix, making contractions stronger.
Ripening apples make ethylene, which makes nearby apples ripen and make more.
Platelets at a wound release chemicals that make more platelets stick there.

items.q: A rare condition stops the alpha cells of the pancreas from releasing glucagon. Insulin release is normal. Predict each change after a 14-hour overnight fast, compared with a healthy person.

variables.name: Breakdown of glycogen in the liver
Number of insulin receptors on muscle cells

items.q: Put the events of the glucose feedback loop after a meal in order.
options: Glucose from the meal raises blood glucose above its normal range.
Beta cells in the pancreas release more insulin.
Muscle and fat cells take up glucose, and the liver stores it as glycogen.
Blood glucose falls back toward its set point.
Insulin release falls as the stimulus fades.

items.q: In the untreated culture, which group of cells is the largest, and in which phase are those cells?
options: Cells with DNA content 1.0, which are in G1
Cells with DNA content 2.0, which are in G2 or mitosis
Cells with DNA content 1.5, which are partway through S
Cells with DNA content 2.0, which are in G1

items.q: What percentage of the untreated cells are partway through S phase (DNA content between 1.0 and 2.0)? Give a whole number.

Which explanation best fits the effect of drug Q?
options: It stops cells from completing mitosis, so cells with copied DNA do not divide.
It stops DNA from being copied, so cells build up before they have finished S phase.
It makes cells copy their DNA a second time, so they build up with extra DNA.
It speeds up G1, so cells reach S phase and copy their DNA sooner than usual.

items.q: A different untreated culture is given drug R, which blocks DNA copying, for 18 hours. Predict how its histogram compares with the untreated one.

More cells at 2.0, and fewer at 1.0, as cells copy their DNA but are unable to divide
The same pattern, because drug R acts once the cells reach mitosis, not before
Cells spread evenly across each DNA content, because S phase takes longer

items.q: Calculate the mitotic index of the root tips grown with the growth chemical. Give a whole-number percentage.

options: Reject the null hypothesis: the difference in mitotic index is unlikely to be due to chance alone.
Fail to reject the null hypothesis, because the chi-square value is larger than the critical value.
The chemical is proven to make root cells divide faster, because the chi-square value is so large.
Reject the null hypothesis, because 70 is larger than 40 in the mitosis column of the table.

items.q: Each group's 200 cells all came from one root tip of one bulb. Which change would most improve the reliability of the comparison?
options: Count cells from several root tips taken from several bulbs in each group.
Count the 200 cells again under a higher magnification for each group.
Count cells from the oldest part of the root, far from the tip, in each group.
Grow the treated bulbs for one day and the control bulbs for three days.

items.q: A higher mitotic index could mean that cells divide more often, or that each mitosis takes longer. Which additional measurement would best tell these apart?
options: The increase in root length over the 3 days in each group
The number of chromosomes in cells at metaphase in each group
The color of the stain in treated and control root tips
The percentage of cells in interphase in each group

items.q: How many sister chromatids does the cell have in G2?

options: 6 chromosomes and 12 pg of DNA
3 chromosomes and 6 pg of DNA
6 chromosomes and 24 pg of DNA
12 chromosomes and 12 pg of DNA

items.q: A drug stops the ring of actin filaments from tightening in animal cells but does not affect mitosis. Predict what dividing cells look like after the drug is added.
options: Single cells with two nuclei, because mitosis finishes but the cytoplasm is not divided
Cells stuck at metaphase, because the chromosomes fail to attach to the spindle
Two daughter cells with one nucleus each, because cytokinesis goes on using a cell plate
Cells with no nucleus, because the chromosomes are lost when the furrow fails

items.q: Why do plant cells divide their cytoplasm by building a cell plate rather than pinching in with a cleavage furrow?
options: The rigid cell wall would resist pinching, so a new wall and membrane are built from the middle outward.
Plant cells have no actin, so the cell plate is the one structure they can assemble from the cytoskeleton.
Plant cells have no spindle, so a cell plate is needed to separate the sister chromatids.
Plant chromosomes are too large to pass through a furrow, so the plate wraps around each set.

items.q: Most adult nerve cells are in G0. Which observation does this help explain?
options: Nerve cells lost after a stroke are not replaced by the division of the surviving ones.
Nerve cells contain less DNA than skin cells, since they skip S phase.
Nerve cells are the fastest-dividing cells of the body after an injury.
Nerve cells have twice as many chromosomes as cells that keep on dividing.

items.q: Select the two processes that depend on mitosis.
options: A hydra grows a bud that breaks off as a small, genetically identical hydra.
Skin cells at the edge of a cut divide and close the wound.
A bacterium copies its circular chromosome and splits into two cells.
A virus makes hundreds of copies of itself inside a host cell.
A red blood cell pushes out its nucleus as it matures.

items.q: A drug that stops DNA copying is added to a culture of dividing cells. Predict each change over the next 12 hours, compared with an untreated culture.

variables.name: DNA content of a cell that was already in G2 when the drug was added
Number of chromosomes in a cell in G1
Fraction of cells with doubled DNA content

items.q: Put the events of mitosis and cytokinesis in order.
options: Chromosomes condense and the spindle starts to form.
The nuclear envelope breaks down and spindle fibers attach to the kinetochores.
Chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell.
Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.
Nuclear envelopes re-form around the two sets of chromosomes.
The cytoplasm divides into two daughter cells.

items.q: Which statement best describes the data?
options: CDK protein stays level, while cyclin builds slowly and drops sharply at each mitosis.
CDK protein and cyclin rise and fall together, both peaking at each mitosis.
Cyclin stays level, while CDK protein builds up slowly over time and drops at each mitosis.
Cyclin and cyclin-CDK activity both stay low except during S phase.

items.q: Using the peaks in cyclin-CDK activity, how long is one cell cycle? Give a whole number of hours.
Which claim is best supported by the data?
options: The timing of cyclin-CDK activity is set by the amount of cyclin, not the amount of CDK.
The timing of cyclin-CDK activity is set by the amount of CDK, not the amount of cyclin.
Cyclin-CDK activity rises steadily with cyclin through interphase, matching its level at each time.
Cyclin-CDK activity is highest in G1, when the cell decides whether to divide.

items.q: The cells are given a form of mitotic cyclin that binds CDK normally but cannot be destroyed. Predict what happens at about 20 hours.
options: The cells enter mitosis, but cyclin-CDK activity stays high and they cannot finish dividing.
The cells skip mitosis and start copying their DNA again, because cyclin is already high.
The cells do not enter mitosis, because a cyclin that resists destruction is unable to bind CDK.
The cells divide normally, because CDK protein, which sets the timing, is not changed.

items.q: The graph shows that high cyclin-CDK activity happens at the same time as entry into mitosis. Which experiment would best test whether that activity causes entry into mitosis?
options: Inject active cyclin-CDK into G2 cells and see whether they enter mitosis early.
Measure cyclin-CDK activity in a second population of synchronized cells over 48 hours.
Count the number of chromosomes in cells at 20 hours and at 42 hours of the experiment.
Measure the amount of CDK protein in nondividing nerve cells kept in G0 for the same time.

items.q: Which statement best describes the response of the two lines to X-rays?
options: Line N cells build up in G1 and increasingly die by apoptosis; line P cells change little in either.
Both lines build up in G1, but just the line P cells go on to die by apoptosis.
Line P cells build up in G1 and die by apoptosis; line N changes little.
Neither line changes after X-rays compared with the cells that were not exposed.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the results in line N?
options: Damaged DNA raises p53, which holds cells at the G1 checkpoint and triggers apoptosis if repair fails.
X-rays destroy cyclins directly, so cells in line N stop wherever they are in the cycle and then they die.
p53 repairs the broken DNA itself, and cells wait in G1 until p53 has finished each repair.
X-rays speed up S phase in line N, so more cells reach G1 sooner and wear out by apoptosis.

items.q: By what percentage did the fraction of line N cells in G1 increase from 0 h to 12 h? Give a whole number.
Line P cells that survive the X-rays keep dividing. Predict how their descendants compare with line N's survivors.
options: They carry more mutations, because damaged DNA was copied, not repaired or removed.
They carry fewer mutations, because without p53 the damaged cells die faster.
They carry the same mutations, because both lines received the same dose of X-rays.
They stop dividing within a day, because damaged DNA is impossible to copy.

items.q: What is the main purpose of the dishes that were not exposed to X-rays?
options: To show that the changes in line N are caused by the X-rays, not by time in culture
To show that line N and line P grow at the same rate when they are not exposed
To give the X-rayed cells somewhere to move when they leave the cycle
To measure how much DNA damage each line can repair without p53

items.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the four results?
options: S-phase and M-phase cytoplasm contains factors that push another nucleus into that phase.
Each nucleus controls its own timing, and the cytoplasm it shares has no effect on it.
The G1 nucleus is the one that controls the timing of both nuclei in a fused cell.
Fusing any two cells makes both nuclei enter mitosis together, in whatever phase each one was in.

items.q: In the S + G2 fusion, the G2 nucleus did not copy its DNA again even though it shared cytoplasm with an S-phase nucleus. Which explanation best fits?
options: Something in a nucleus that has already copied its DNA blocks a second round of copying in the same cycle.
The G2 nucleus had too little cyclin of its own to respond to any signal coming from the S-phase cytoplasm.
The S-phase factor does not reach a G2 nucleus, because G2 nuclei have no pores in their nuclear envelope.
The G2 nucleus was damaged by the fusion, so it waited for repair at the G2 checkpoint before mitosis.

items.q: The M-phase factor is now known to be MPF, an active cyclin-CDK complex. Before fusion with a G2 cell, the M-phase cell is treated with a drug that blocks CDK kinase activity. Predict the result.
options: The G2 nucleus does not condense its chromosomes, because the factor that drives mitosis is inactive.
The G2 nucleus condenses its chromosomes as before, because the M-phase cell's cyclin is still present.
The G2 nucleus copies its DNA again, because blocking CDK sends the cell back to S phase.
The G2 nucleus condenses even faster, because the drug frees cyclin to act on the nucleus itself.

items.q: Some cancer drugs block the CDKs that work with G1 cyclins. Based on the fusion results and what you know of the cycle, predict their effect on cancer cells that depend on these CDKs.
options: The cells are held at the G1 checkpoint and do not start copying their DNA.
The cells are held in mitosis, because their chromosomes are unable to finish separating.
The cells copy their DNA twice before dividing, because G1 is skipped.
The cells divide faster, because they spend less time waiting in G1.

items.q: Why can a mutation in one copy of a proto-oncogene promote cancer, while a tumor suppressor gene usually must lose both copies?
options: An overactive accelerator works despite a normal copy; one working brake copy still makes enough brake protein.
Proto-oncogenes are found on one chromosome of each pair, while tumor suppressor genes are found on both of them.
Tumor suppressor genes are copied twice in S phase, while proto-oncogenes are copied once each cycle.
Mutations in proto-oncogenes are passed to daughter cells, while those in tumor suppressor genes are not.

items.q: Normal skin cells in a dish have stopped dividing in a single layer. A strip of cells is scraped away. Predict what happens.
options: Cells at the edges divide and fill the strip, then stop when they touch neighbors on all sides.
Cells across the whole dish start dividing and pile up in layers, because the contact signal is lost.
No cells divide, because cells that have stopped once by contact inhibition remain in G0 for good.
Cells at the edges die by apoptosis, because losing their neighbors damages their DNA.

items.q: A tumor removed from a patient's colon is described as malignant. Which finding would best support that description?
options: Cells from the tumor are found invading the colon wall and growing in the liver.
The tumor is made of cells that are dividing faster than normal colon cells.
The tumor is surrounded by a capsule and has stayed the same size for a year.
The tumor's cells have a nucleus and copy their DNA before they divide.

items.q: Select the two changes that would make uncontrolled cell division more likely.
options: A mutation that makes a growth factor receptor active without its growth factor
Loss of both working copies of the p53 gene
A mutation that makes a G1 cyclin get destroyed faster
An extra working copy of a tumor suppressor gene
A drug that switches on caspases in the cell

items.q: In a line of cells, the M checkpoint no longer works: anaphase starts on schedule whether or not every chromosome is attached to the spindle. Predict each change, compared with normal cells.

variables.name: Chance that a daughter cell gets the wrong number of chromosomes
Time a cell spends in metaphase when one chromosome is slow to attach
Amount of DNA copied in S phase
Number of centrosomes formed before mitosis

items.q: Put the events of a cell's response to severe DNA damage in G1 in order.
options: Radiation breaks the cell's DNA.
p53 protein builds up in the cell.
p53 switches on a gene for a protein that blocks cyclin-CDK.
The cycle halts at the G1 checkpoint while repair is attempted.
Repair fails, and p53 switches on genes that trigger apoptosis.
Caspases take the cell apart.
